title: Explain the JVM internals: the memory areas (heap, stack, metaspace, code cache), how garbage collection works, what the JIT compiler does, and how you analyze thread dumps, heap dumps, and GC logs when troubleshooting a production Java service.
shortTitle: JVM Internals: Memory areas, GC, JIT, thread dump analysis
keyPoints: The heap stores all objects created with new and is split into Young Generation (Eden + Survivors) and Old Generation
Each thread has its own stack holding method frames, local variables, and return addresses
Metaspace (replacing PermGen in Java 8) stores class metadata in native memory and grows automatically
The JIT compiler detects hot methods and compiles them to native code using tiered compilation (C1 quick, C2 heavy)
Minor GC cleans the Young Generation cheaply; Full GC cleans the Old Generation with longer pauses
jstack shows thread state for deadlock detection; jmap captures heap dumps for Eclipse MAT analysis
In containers, always set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 so the JVM respects container memory limits

s1_definition.oneliner: The heap stores objects and the garbage collector cleans it, each thread gets its own stack, metaspace holds class metadata, and the JIT compiler turns hot bytecode into fast native machine code.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Heap** – the shared memory area where all objects created with `new` live; managed by the garbage collector and split into Young and Old generations.
- **Stack** – per-thread memory holding method frames, local variables, and return addresses; grows and shrinks as methods are called and return.
- **Metaspace** – stores class metadata (class structure, method definitions); replaced PermGen in Java 8 and grows automatically in native memory.
- **Code cache** – stores native machine code produced by the JIT compiler for hot methods.
- **JIT compiler** – converts frequently executed bytecode into optimized native code at runtime using tiered compilation (C1 and C2).
- **Garbage collector** – automatically reclaims memory from objects no longer reachable, using generational collection.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of the JVM as the National Bank of India head office building. The heap is the giant records vault where all customer files (objects) are stored, and a cleanup crew (garbage collector) regularly removes files no one references. Each bank teller (thread) has their own small desk (stack) for the one customer they are serving. The rulebook room (metaspace) stores what a Savings Account or Trade even is. And a fast-lane counter (code cache) pre-prepares forms for the most frequent transactions so they do not have to be filled from scratch each time.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The JVM divides memory into several areas, and understanding them is essential for debugging production issues. The heap is where all objects live and is managed by the garbage collector, split into a Young Generation for short-lived objects and an Old Generation for long-lived ones. Minor GC cleans the Young Generation cheaply, while Full GC cleans the Old Generation with longer pauses. Each thread has its own stack for method frames, metaspace holds class metadata, and the code cache holds native code from the JIT compiler.

The JIT compiler is what makes Java fast in production. The JVM interprets bytecode at first, and when it sees a hot method running thousands of times it compiles it to native code using tiered compilation. The C1 compiler does quick optimization and the C2 compiler does heavy optimization including inlining and escape analysis. A tight fee-calculation loop over millions of trades runs close to native speed after warm-up.

When a service misbehaves in production, I reach for specific tools. I take a thread dump with jstack to find blocked or deadlocked threads. I capture a heap dump with jmap and open it in Eclipse MAT to find memory leaks. I enable GC logging to see pause times and collection frequency. For deeper profiling I use Java Flight Recorder because of its low overhead.

The single most important production habit in the banking systems at National Bank of India is controlling the heap size in containers using the MaxRAMPercentage flag, so the JVM respects the container's memory limit rather than seeing the entire host. Getting that wrong is a very common cause of containers being killed.

Remember one sentence: the heap stores objects and the GC cleans them generationally, the JIT compiles hot bytecode to native speed, and jstack, jmap, and GC logs are the three tools that diagnose production issues.
